title: Optimizing inference for voice models in production - Philip Kiely, Baseten

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core subject is serving trained TTS models in production using TensorRT-LLM, FP8 quantization, KV cache engineering, dynamic batching, and latency optimization. Baseten is a model inference platform for software builders, and the optimization techniques apply cross-domain to any team deploying voice models. The content addresses production deployment and serving optimization of already-trained models. Requires familiarity with LLM inference concepts, quantization, and GPU architecture but remains accessible to practicing engineers. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. summary: Philip Kiely leads Developer Relations at Baseten, a model inference platform serving AI-native startups and enterprises. His talk focuses on optimizing inference for voice models in production, using Orpheus TTS from Canopy Labs as the primary example. Orpheus is built on a Llama 3.2 3B backbone with a larger vocabulary for speech-specific tokens and extended context length via rope scaling. Because of this LLM architecture, standard LLM optimization tools apply. Key performance metrics include time to first byte (TTFB), tokens per second, and throughput. Unlike general LLM optimization where maximizing TPS is the goal, voice models only need about 83 TPS for real-time streaming; beyond that, the focus shifts to minimizing TTFB and maximizing concurrency to fit many simultaneous streams on minimal GPU resources. Optimization techniques include TensorRT-LLM for runtime, FP8 quantization (including KV cache) on Hopper architecture, torch compile and PyTorch inference mode on the audio decoder (snac), dynamic batching with a 15ms timeout, and support for multiple streaming protocols. The implementation is often CPU-bound, not GPU-bound. Results on an H100 MIG (half an H100) show 16 simultaneous streams with variable traffic and 24 with constant traffic, achieving 150ms TTFB. However, non-runtime factors—infrastructure choices like region routing and client code patterns like session establishment—can easily add back hundreds of milliseconds, negating runtime gains. The talk concludes with practical client code guidance: production usage should employ a multiprocess pool with shared sessions rather than sequential requests. For voice pipelines, protocols like websockets or gRPC (which Baseten supports) may be preferable to HTTP streaming. Kiely frames voice agents as three components—listening, thinking, talking—where TTS is only one part. Infrastructure connecting these components, such as co-locating models in the same data center and avoiding DNS hairpins, is equally or more important than runtime optimization. Even small per-step savings (10ms) compound across 4-5 pipeline steps, potentially consuming 10% of the SLA. Future topics not covered include fine-tuning, voice cloning, and audio artifact removal.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Agenda
sections.summary: Philip Kiely introduces himself from Baseten, a model inference platform. He outlines the agenda: TTS model architecture, performance metrics, optimization techniques, measurement, and infrastructure/client code considerations.

sections.title: TTS Model Architecture
sections.summary: Explains that TTS models like Orpheus are architecturally similar to LLMs, using a Llama 3.2 3B backbone. This enables reuse of LLM optimization tooling. Orpheus has a larger vocab for speech tokens and extended context length via rope scaling.

sections.title: Performance Metrics and Goals
sections.summary: Discusses TTFB, tokens per second, and throughput. Unlike general LLMs where maximizing TPS is the goal, voice models only need ~83 TPS for real-time streaming. Beyond that, focus shifts to minimizing TTFB and maximizing concurrency to fit many streams on fewer GPUs.

sections.title: Optimization Techniques
sections.summary: Covers TensorRT-LLM, FP8 quantization including KV cache on Hopper architecture, torch compile and PyTorch inference mode on snac audio decoder, dynamic batching with 15ms timeout, and multiple streaming protocol support. Notes the implementation is often CPU-bound.

sections.title: Results and Benchmarks
sections.summary: On an H100 MIG (half H100), the optimized implementation supports 16 streams with variable traffic and 24 with constant traffic, achieving 150ms TTFB. Cost works out to a few cents per hour of conversation at scale, substantially better than per-token API pricing.

sections.title: Non-Runtime Factors and Pitfalls
sections.summary: Transitions to discussing how infrastructure and client code can negate runtime gains. Pitfalls include routing queries to wrong regions and establishing new sessions on each request, which can add back hundreds of milliseconds of latency.

sections.title: Client Code, Pipeline Architecture, and Conclusion
sections.summary: Recommends production client code using a multiprocess pool with shared sessions instead of sequential requests (available on Baseten GitHub). Notes support for websockets and gRPC protocols alongside HTTP streaming. Frames voice agents as three parts—listening, thinking, talking—where TTS is only one. Emphasizes that infrastructure connecting models (data center co-location, DNS hairpin avoidance) is equally important to runtime optimization, as small per-step savings compound across 4-5 pipeline steps. Mentions upcoming event and contact information.
